CD19+ B-cell depletion was demonstrated with median repletion time of ~110 weeks in both rituximab arms, confirming that rituximab successfully engaged CD20 on B-cells and depleted them. Post-rituximab low immunoglobulin concentration increased from 0.2% to 5.1%, consistent with B-cell depletion. 2. PATHWAY MODULATION: Downstream biology clearly moved. CRP decreased ~27.5% (2x0.5g) and ~23.1% (2x1.0g) vs increased 58.1% in placebo. ESR decreased ~28-29% in rituximab arms vs increased 8% in placebo. DAS28-ESR improved by -1.71 and -1.68 in rituximab arms vs -0.76 in placebo. These inflammatory biomarkers confirm that B-cell depletion translated into suppression of autoimmune inflammation. 3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: The primary endpoint was met. ACR20 at Week 24 was 54.5% (2x0.5g) and 50.6% (2x1.0g) vs 23.3% (placebo), representing a ~31 percentage point treatment difference. Secondary endpoints also supported efficacy: ACR50 26.3% and 25.9% vs 9.3%; EULAR Good Response 17.4% and 11.8% vs 4.7%; DAS28 clinical remission 9.6% and 9.4% vs 2.3%. The effect size is clinically meaningful. 4. POPULATION EFFECTS: Both rituximab doses showed similar efficacy, suggesting the mechanism is robust across dose levels in this population. HAQ-DI improvement was also observed (66.1% and 58.2% vs 47.7%), indicating functional benefit. No subgroup analysis identified differential responders, suggesting broad population benefit. 5. CONFOUNDERS: The placebo response rate of 23.3% ACR20 is moderate but not unusually high for RA trials. The trial was adequately powered (n=511). Safety signals (serious infections, prolonged B-cell depletion, hypogammaglobulinemia) are consistent with the mechanism but did not prevent adequate dosing or compromise the efficacy readout. No dose-limiting toxicity prevented target engagement. The trial is a clean success with strong mechanistic validation across the entire causal chain.
